title: Why O(n)?
prompt: The monotonic stack has a while-loop inside a for-loop. Why is it still O(n) overall?
options: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once — total stack operations ≤ 2n
It's actually O(n²) but fast in practice
explanation: Amortized analysis: charge each pop to the element being popped, not to the current iteration. Total pops ≤ total pushes = n.

title: Drill: remove adjacent duplicates
prompt: From memory: repeatedly delete adjacent equal pairs — `"abbaca"` → remove `bb` → `"aaca"` → remove `aa` → `"ca"`. Stack version: for each char, if it equals the top, pop; else push. Build the answer with StringBuilder from the stack bottom (hint: use the deque as a stack but a StringBuilder works as the stack itself!).

solution.explanation: A StringBuilder IS a char stack: append = push, deleteCharAt(last) = pop, charAt(last) = peek — and the final answer needs no reversal.

hints: A deletion can make two earlier characters adjacent. Which character does each new char need to be compared against?
Compare with the most recently kept character — treat the StringBuilder as a stack.
Equal to the last char → `deleteCharAt(len - 1)`; otherwise `append(c)`.

title: Drill: next greater element (monotonic stack)
prompt: From memory (monotonic stack of indices): for each element, return the next greater element to its RIGHT, or -1 if none.

solution.explanation: The stack holds indices still waiting for a greater element, in decreasing value order; a new value pops exactly the ones it beats. Anything never popped keeps -1. Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

hints: When a big number arrives, which earlier elements has it just "answered"?
Keep indices of elements still waiting for an answer; a new value resolves every waiting element smaller than it.

title: RPN: operand order
prompt: Complete the subtraction case and the number case of the RPN evaluator.
explanation: The operand pushed last is popped first, so the first pop is the RIGHT operand `b`. `["5","3","-"]` must give `5 - 3 = 2`, i.e. `a - b`. Numbers are parsed with `Integer.parseInt`.

title: Template recall: monotonic stack
prompt: From memory: Daily Temperatures — days until a warmer temperature.
explanation: The stack holds indices of days still waiting for a warmer day. `temps[i]` resolves every waiting day colder than it (`peek` to compare, `pop` to resolve) with distance `i - idx`, then waits itself. O(n) amortized.

title: Drill: previous smaller element index
prompt:
From memory: for each `i`, return the index of the nearest element to the LEFT that is **strictly smaller** than `nums[i]`, or -1 if none. This is the "left boundary" half of Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

`[3,1,4,2,5]` → `[-1,-1,1,1,3]`

tests.note: increasing: the previous index every time

solution.explanation: Any earlier element >= nums[i] can never be the "previous smaller" for i or anything after i (nums[i] is closer and no larger), so pop it. What remains on top is the answer. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n) time, O(n) space.

hints: If an earlier element is at least as big as nums[i], can it ever be the answer for any index at or after i?
Keep a stack of indices with increasing values; discard ones that are no longer useful before reading the answer.
`while (!st.isEmpty() && nums[st.peek()] >= nums[i]) st.pop();` then the top (or -1) is the answer.
